response:
Team,

Our branching model is quietly costing us more than we admit, and it's time to switch to trunk-based development.

## The problem

Long-lived feature branches let work drift apart for weeks before it ever meets. By the time we merge, conflicts are large, context is stale, and integration bugs surface far from where they were introduced.

- Merge weeks routinely cost two to three days of rework across the team, based on our last four release retros.
- Code review happens on branches nobody else can safely build on top of, so reviewers approve in isolation and surprises appear only at merge time.

## The proposal

Trunk-based development means everyone commits small, reviewed changes to main at least daily, behind feature flags when work is incomplete.

- Adopt feature flags for anything that can't ship complete in a day, so main stays releasable at all times.
- Cap any branch's lifetime at one day; longer efforts get flagged and merged incrementally instead of branched.
- Pair the switch with faster CI, targeting under ten minutes, so small, frequent merges don't bottleneck on pipeline time.

## What could go wrong

The strongest objection is real: without discipline, trunk-based development can expose half-finished work to production risk, and feature flags themselves become technical debt if we never retire them. A team of twelve juggling flags across several in-flight features could end up with tangled conditional logic that's harder to reason about than clean branches ever were. We should take this seriously rather than dismiss it — it means adopting an explicit flag-cleanup policy and naming someone accountable for auditing stale flags monthly, not just trusting that good habits will hold under deadline pressure.

There is also a real ramp-up cost worth naming: for the first few weeks, engineers used to isolated branches will feel more exposed reviewing smaller, faster-moving changes, and we should expect some friction and a temporary dip in velocity before the benefits show up.

I would like a decision by the end of next week.
